The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{n}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2n & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

We start by proving the base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2(1) & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2k & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the **inductive step**.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k+1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2(k+1) & 1\end{aligned}].\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving matrix identities using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to factor out one instance of the matrix, as follows:

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k+1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k+1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

By the inductive hypothesis

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{k}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2k & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2k+2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2(k+1) & 1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction,
${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{n}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2n & 1\end{aligned}]$
is true for all $n\in N.$
